chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from Muhammad ibn Ali, from Muhammad ibn al-Fudayl, from Abu Hamza al-Thumali, who said:

I was sitting in the Mosque of the Messenger (peace be upon him and his family) when a man approached, greeted, and asked, 'Who are you, O servant of Allah?' I said, 'A man from the people of Kufa.' He asked, 'What is your need?' I said to him, 'Do you know Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Ali (peace be upon him)?' I said, 'Yes.' He said, 'What is your need to him?' He said, 'I have prepared forty questions to ask him about them; whatever is truth I will take, and whatever is falsehood I will leave.' Abu Hamza said, 'So I said to him, 'Do you know the difference between truth and falsehood?' He said, 'Yes.' I said to him, 'Then what is your need for him if you know the difference between truth and falsehood?' He said to me, 'O people of Kufa! You are a people who cannot be tolerated. When you see Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), inform me.'

My speech with him did not cease until Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) approached, and around him were the people of Khurasan and others, asking him about the rituals of Hajj. He proceeded until he sat in his place, and the man sat near him. Abu Hamza said, 'So I sat where I could hear the speech, and around him was a multitude of people. When he had fulfilled their needs and they departed, he turned to the man and said to him, 'Who are you?' He said, 'I am Qatada ibn Di'ama al-Basri.' Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said to him, 'You are a jurist of the people of Basra?' He said, 'Yes.'

Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said to him, 'Woe to you, O Qatada! Indeed, Allah, Glorious and Mighty, created a people from His creation and made them proofs upon His creation. They are the pegs in His earth, standing by His command, excellent in His knowledge. He chose them before creating them as shades on the right of His Throne.'

Qatada was silent for a long time, then said, 'May Allah rectify you! By Allah, I have sat before the jurists and in front of Ibn Abbas, and my heart did not tremble before any of them as it trembled before you.' Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said to him, 'Woe to you! Do you know where you are? You are in front of houses which Allah has permitted to be exalted and that His Name be mentioned in them; glorifying Him therein in the mornings and the evenings. Men whom neither trade nor selling diverts from the remembrance of Allah and the establishing of prayer and the giving of zakat. So you are there, and we are those [men].'

Qatada said to him, 'You have spoken the truth, by Allah. May Allah make me a ransom for you! By Allah, they are not houses of stone nor of clay.' Qatada said, 'So inform me about cheese.' He smiled, then said, 'Your questions have returned to this.' He said, 'It is lost upon me.' He said, 'There is no problem with it.' He said, 'Indeed, sometimes rennet of the dead is put in it.' He said, 'There is no problem with it. Indeed, the rennet has no veins, nor is there blood in it, nor does it have bone; it merely emerges from between the dung and blood.'

Then he said, 'And the rennet is like a dead chicken from which an egg is extracted; would you eat that egg?' Qatada said, 'No, and I would not instruct in eating it.' He said to him, 'And why?' He said, 'Because it is from the dead.' He said to him, 'So if that egg is incubated and a chicken comes out of it, would you eat it?' He said, 'Yes.' He said, 'So what prohibited the egg for you and permitted the chicken for you?'

Then he (peace be upon him) said, 'So the rennet is like the egg. So buy the cheese from the markets of the Muslims, from the hands of the praying ones, and do not ask about it except if there comes to you one who informs you about it.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on cheese containing rennet from the dead in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Kafi* highlights the intellectual encounter between Qatada ibn Di'ama, a prominent Basran jurist, and Imam Muhammad ibn al-Alq (the Fourth Imam), illustrating the transition from rational jurisprudence to divine authority. The Imam first establishes his status as the 'pegs of the earth' by quoting Quran 24:36-37, then employs a logical analogy regarding an egg from a dead chicken to clarify the purity of rennet (*infaḥa*) in cheese, demonstrating the Shia method of deriving practical legal rulings through precise textual and rational analysis.
